targetAudience.primary: Architects, security engineers, and governance owners building multi-agent or digital-employee runtimes
targetAudience.knowledgeAssumption: The reader understands tool permissions, shared state, delegation, and recovery at a practical systems level.
targetAudience.readerProblem: Local worker checks are being treated as evidence that the end-to-end system is safe even when influence can move through shared state, handoffs, delegated authority, or recovery.

whyNow: A 2026 systematization of 197 multi-agent security works and a separate audit of 44 evaluation works organizes attacks and defenses around execution paths, observation, intervention, trust boundaries, and recovery, making the gap between local safety and system-level closure unusually explicit.

externalHook.description: Every local transition can look allowed while untrusted influence still reaches a protected effect through another route.

coreProposition: Multi-agent safety is an end-to-end authority-to-effect property, not the sum of local worker checks: a credible safety claim needs provenance-preserving route evidence, stated observation and intervention coverage, explicit trust assumptions, alternate-route assessment, and verified recovery of derivative state and authority.

originalValue.description: Turns the source framework into an auditable engineering question: what evidence closes the complete route from influence origin to protected effect, including alternate paths and post-containment recovery?

readerTakeaway: Treat local permission checks as one layer of evidence; bind protected effects to origin-to-effect lineage, record blind spots and trust assumptions, and separate containment from recovery.

supported: The primary systematization covers 197 works and separately audits 44 evaluation works.
The source organizes multi-agent security around interaction interfaces, recurring attack paths, and defense fields including observation, intervention, trust boundary, and recovery.
The evidence supports distinguishing local protection from end-to-end path closure and containment from recovery.
unsupported: That any concrete production runtime has closed every authority-to-effect path
A universal topology, trust model, or authorization algorithm
Unlimited centralized telemetry as the correct observability design
uncertain: How to preserve trustworthy provenance through compaction without excessive surveillance
How to test dynamic alternate-route closure online
Which derivative effects require prevention versus compensating recovery

firstPartyRole.rationale: The article is based on public primary research and is independently useful to multi-agent security practitioners without first-party project references.

decisionReason: The source and same-date analysis support a bounded, actionable system-level security model without claiming universal closure or implementation proof.
